newsitem.title: GREECE: Greece needs policy changes to head off trade woes.
newsitem.headline: Greece needs policy changes to head off trade woes.

text.p: The deterioration of Greece's trade and current account in the first quarter of this year is not an immediate cause of concern, but corrective measures are needed in the long-run, bankers said on Friday.

"The current account and trade deficits do not pose a problem at this point but they should be dealt with to avoid permanent damage to the production base and the fostering of expectations of a sharp devaluation of the drachma in the future," said a senior banker at a foreign bank.
Greece's cumulative current account deficit rose 35.2 percent year-on-year to $1.63 billion in the first quarter of this year on the back of a larger trade deficit of $4.84 billion, up 11.9 percent.

But the current account deficit for the month of March alone fell a surprising 16.2 percent year-on-year to $753 million because a larger invisibles surplus more than offset a 4.6 percent rise in the trade deficit.
Greece's current account deficit rose to $4.54 billion or 3.8 percent of GDP in 1996 from $2.85 billion or 2.7 percent of GDP in 1995.

"The widening of the current account deficit reflects a faster GDP growth, a loss in competitiveness and the continuing resort of local corporates to cheaper foreign borrowing," said Michalis Masourakis, manager at the research division of private Alpha Credit Bank.

Government forecasts project Greek GDP will grow by 3.5 percent this year, versus 2.6 percent in 1996, boosted by strong domestic investment. Gross investment spending is forecast to jump 22 percent in 1997 from an estimated 9.3 percent in 1996.
Government officials have partly attributed the wider trade deficit to imports of capital goods needed to satisfy a strong domestic investment boom.
Some economists have blamed the central bank's hard drachma policy for the loss of competitiveness that has led to increased import penetration and the stagnation of exports.

They define competitiveness in terms of the real exchange rate -- the nominal exchange rate adjusted for inflation differentials -- and say that the drachma has appreciated in real terms against the currencies of Greece's major trading partners.

The central bank wants to keep the drachma broadly stable against the major currencies that make up the ecu in its quest for a lower inflation of 4.5 percent by end-97 and below 3.0 percent by end-1998. Inflation currently stands at 5.5 percent.

But others have countered that the benefits from the strong drachma policy outweigh costs by putting a lid on the prices of imported goods and raw materials entering the production process, holding down inflationary expectations and providing cheaper foreign currency for local corporations.

"The hard drachma policy is not the root cause of the trade and current account deficit," said an economist at a foreign bank. "The exchange rate is an important part of the mechanism that translates changes in desired capital inflows into changes in the trade balance."
Product quality, good distribution networks and marketing are also crucial for an export drive that would relieve the trade and the current account balances, he added.
"The hard drachma policy might hurt traditional exports that are labour-intensive but not high value-added goods and services," the economist said.

Masourakis added, "The cheaper foreign currency borrowing has weakened the resolve of local corporates to resist wage demands, therefore leading to higher unit labour costs, a loss of competitiveness and a rise in imports."
He added that other economists see the budget deficit as the prime source of the trade deficit.

The general government budget deficit fell to 7.4 percent of GDP in 1996 and the offical government budget target for this year is 4.2 percent of GDP but bankers and international organisations have attributed part of the improvement to creative accounting.

"Window-dressing can give a lower ratio of budget deficit to GDP but it does not help much in limiting the growth of public debt and constraining aggregate demand growth and increasing national savings," he said.
"A country where aggregate spending keeps on rising faster than nominal income is bound to have a widening trade deficit."
Bankers also pointed out that the balance of payments only counts transactions in foreign currencies and understates the effects of exports which are paid for in drachmas.

"The current methodology does not take into account Greece's trade transactions with neighbouring countries denominated in drachmas, thus overestimating the actual size of the trade gap," said Masourakis.

Provisional estimates put net exports to these countries at $1.0 billion or more a year. But central bank officials caution that even if those exports were fully captured in the trade balance there might not be a comparable improvement in the current account balance because there might be an offsetting change in invisibles calculations.
"This is because we suspect that we capture part of the drachma denominated trade flows in the invisibles balance under the current methodology," an official said. -- Athens Newsroom +301 3311812-4
